facts.statement: The type species Anatalavis rex was discovered in Hornerstown, New Jersey, with remains collected in 1869 and 1878.
facts.quote: The type species Anatalavis rex is known from Hornerstown, New Jersey, and its remains were collected by J.G.Meirs in 1869 and W.Ross in 1878.

facts.statement: Storrs L. Olson and David C. Parris established the genus Anatalavis in 1987, naming it "duck-winged bird" to reflect its affinity to waterfowl.
facts.quote: Its affinity to waterfowl was only recognized in 1987 by Storrs L. Olson and David C. Parris, who consequently established the genus Anatalavis, meaning "duck-winged bird", from Latin anas "duck", ala "wing" and avis "bird".

facts.statement: Anatalavis rex is known only from two humeri, a right wing and a left wing, which lack the proximal end.
facts.quote: A. rex is only known from two humeri (holotype YPM 902 of a right wing, and paratype YPM 948 of a left wing) which are distinct and characteristic even though they lack the proximal end.

facts.statement: The humerus of Anatalavis rex has a pronounced curve in its shaft, unlike the straight shaft found in the related genus Telmatornis.
facts.quote: Notably, the shaft of the humerus has a pronounced curve like in living ducks; in the original humerus fossils of Telmatornis little of the shaft was preserved, but eventually a more complete specimen was discovered, and its straight shaft is quite unlike that of Anatalavis.

facts.statement: The living Anatalavis rex was likely similar in bulk to an average-sized dabbling duck of the genus Anas.
facts.quote: the living bird was probably similar to an average-sized dabbling duck of genus Anas in bulk.

facts.statement: The species Anatalavis oxfordi was described by Olson about 80 years after A. rex, based on fossils found in the London Clay Bed A at Walton-on-the-Naze, England, and named after collector Andrew Oxford.
facts.quote: Some 80 years after A. rex, a second species Anatalavis oxfordi was described by Olson, based on fossils found in the earliest Eocene (Ypresian age, about 55 mya) London Clay Bed A at Walton-on-the-Naze, England, and named in honor of the collector Andrew Oxford of Great Mongeham, Kent, who donated the fossil for scientific research.

facts.statement: Jiří Mlíkovský controversially proposed in 2002 that Anatalavis oxfordi should be placed in the separate genus Nettapterornis due to differences in the humerus angle compared to A. rex.
facts.quote: Jiří Mlíkovský in 2002 disagreed with uniting A. oxfordi with the considerably older A. rex and pointed out that the distal end of the humerus seems to be set at a slightly different angle relative to the bone's shaft in the two species. He thus established the genus Nettapterornis – with the same meaning as Anatalavis but in Ancient Greek, from netta (νεττα), pteron (πτερον) and ornis (ορνις) – for A. oxfordi, but this remains controversial.

facts.statement: It remains unresolved whether Anatalavis belongs to modern waterfowl or to a basal lineage like Conflictonidae that evolved a filter-feeding beak independently.
facts.quote: Thus, whether Anatalavis was indeed a member of the modern waterfowl, or belongs to a basal lineage – possibly family Conflictonidae – that evolved a filter-feeding beak in parallel to today's ducks and geese, is as unresolved as ever.

facts.statement: The fossils of Anatalavis rex are likely from the Hornerstown Formation around 66 million years ago, though their exact age relative to the K-Pg boundary is debated due to reworked deposits.
facts.quote: They are probably from the Hornerstown Formation (Late Cretaceous or Early Paleocene, some 66 million years ago) – usually, they are assumed to be from the lower Maastrichtian layer of the Hornerstown Formation, but they might be younger and postdate the Mesozoic, or even from the slightly older Navesink Formation, as these deposits are reworked and locally mixed across the K-Pg boundary, and no exact locality data was recorded for the A. rex fossils.

facts.statement: Anatalavis oxfordi is known from a partial skeleton found in the earliest Eocene London Clay, which was well-preserved but delicate and broken.
facts.quote: This species is known from a partial skeleton, one of the best-preserved London Clay fossils at the time it was found, but in a delicate state of preservation and much broken.

facts.statement: A 2019 analysis rejected with some confidence the hypothesis that Anatalavis is closer to living ducks than to the magpie-goose, though it cannot fully exclude this possibility.
facts.quote: the hypothesis that it is even closer to living ducks than the magpie-goose, however, seems to be an artifact of the small sample of taxa analyzed by Dyke in 1999: the 2019 analysis rejects it with some confidence, even though it cannot exclude it at a high level of certainty.

rejected.statement: Anatalavis is a genus of prehistoric birds related to ducks and geese, possibly specifically to the magpie-goose.
rejected.quote: Anatalavis is genus of prehistoric birds related to ducks and geese, perhaps to the magpie-goose (Anseranas semipalmata) in particular.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'genus of prehistoric birds related to ducks and'

rejected.statement: A 2019 analysis suggested with low confidence that Anatalavis oxfordi forms a distinct lineage outside living waterfowl, possibly closely related to Conflicto antarcticus.
rejected.quote: A more comprehensive cladistic analysis conducted at that time, comparing a wide range of living and fossil waterfowl and their closest relatives, found C. antarcticus and A. oxfordi to be possibly (but with very low confidence) very closely related and together forming one distinct lineage outside the group of living waterfowl (including the magpie-goose).
